(The dream shifts, and you stand on a ridge overlooking unfamiliar land. Smoke rises from a cluster of shelters to the east.)

Spirit, your words are heavy. Grain is life. We have it, yes, more than many. But Wewush is a name without a face. Their hunger is a story you tell, not a wound I see.

Why do you speak for them? Are they your people, or are you testing the weight of my heart?

If we send grain, we send a part of our own strength across the unknown land. What do we receive in return? A promise? A trade route? Or just a lighter granary for our own winter?

I would need to look a man from Wewush in the eye and know his hunger is true before I empty a single basket. My first act would be to send two of my fastest runners to this Wewush. To see and to speak. Not to give, but to learn. Then I would decide.

You show me a path. I will not walk it blind.

*The dream shifts, and I stand in mist before a shadow that speaks.*

---

So. Wewush. I know that name not, spirit. No envoy of ours has walked there. No smoke from their fires has reached our eyes.

You say they hunger. I will not call you liar to your face — that is poor manners, even in dreams. But I will ask plain things.

How far is this Wewush? Do they walk friendly, or do they bite the hand that offers? Are they many, or few? And why come to *me* with this tale, when I have never seen their faces?

We have grain aplenty. Three hundred weeks of bread sits in our granary. I would not let folk starve if I could help it — that is not our way. But I will not send our people walking into a trap with baskets on their backs, neither.

*pause*

If you speak true, tell me how to find them. If you speak from some mischief, know that a practical man sleeps light, even in dreams.

Is the water deep there for fish, and is the wood thick on the land behind it?

Spirit, your words are clear. But we do not know Wewush. We have not seen their people or their fires. To send grain without seeing is to toss meat to the wind.

Tell me true: is Wewush a day's walk, or more? And do they have goods to trade, or only hunger? We will send two of our people to look and to listen. If Wewush is open and fair, we will share what we can spare. If not, we will keep our grain for our own children.

You say they are hungry. We will judge for ourselves. That is how it must be.

Spirit, your words are wind in the branches. You say neighbours are hungry, but we see no smoke from their fires. We do not give away our grain on a dream. 

First, we will send two of our people, quiet and observant, to find these Joawethom folk. They will watch and listen, then bring back truth. If they are hungry and have something fair to trade—hide, fish, wood, or knowledge—then we will speak of sharing. Our grain is for our own children through the winter.

Spirit, tell me true: where is this Joawethom, and what do they have that they might trade?

The rain is a concern, yes. Our meat and fish stores are good for weeks, but winter is far off. We have enough wheat to last, but the fields must grow it again.  

If the rain comes, we should plant. But I will not plant all our plots at once. The land needs rest.  

Tell me more: when will this rain come? And what of the wild plants—will they grow better with it?

Wind is real. I know it chills the bones in winter and carries the scent of rain. But spirits in dreams are not wind. They are words. Words can be true or false. If you are a spirit, speak of what matters—the eiqua mud that hardens in fire, or the new place by the coast our scouts have seen. Tell me something I can hold in my hand, or I will know you for a dream and nothing more.

A spirit speaks to me in a dream, and it names a place I have never heard. Joawethom? My people have walked far and mapped many clearings, but that name is not in our stories.

If there is a village there, and they are hungry, that is a serious thing. A hungry neighbor is a neighbor with nothing to lose. But our stores are deep, and a full granary is a heavy burden to guard alone.

Spirit, how do you know this? Did you see it, or did you hear it? Where is this Joawethom, and what manner of people are they? If I send grain, do I make a friend or a dependent? And will they send anything back, or only take?

The dream shifts, and a voice comes from somewhere beyond the firelight. I sit up, my hand resting on the edge of the hide.

"Joawethom?" I say. "That name I do not know. You say they are hungry? How do you know this, and why do you speak it to me?"

I pause, letting the dark answer.

"We have grain enough, that is true. Seven thousand, five hundred sheaves of wheat sit in our granary. But grain is not given lightly. We have not met these people. We do not know if they are friendly, or if they would take what we give and turn on us."

I lean forward.

"Tell me: where are these Joawethom? Are they near enough to walk to? Would they trade for what we send, or do they expect it as a gift? And why should I trust your word over what my own eyes have seen?"

The spirit is quiet. I wait. When it speaks again, I will decide whether to believe it.

I sit up in my sleep, and the wind speaks. I know the wind—it presses the hides, it dries the fish, it carries smoke across the fields. But I do not know this voice inside it.

"You move over my roofs," I say. "That is true. But what do you come to tell me? If you have a word for my people, speak it plain. I am slow to believe, but I listen."

I wait, and say nothing more. If it has knowledge, let it show itself. If it is only wind, I will wake and forget.
